Minimalism: A Subtle Yet Engaging Experience

Minimalism is a unique puzzle game that embraces simplicity in both design and gameplay, offering a calm yet engaging experience. The game’s premise is straightforward: players must solve puzzles by arranging shapes and colors in a way that creates visually pleasing patterns or meets certain criteria. The minimalistic design allows players to focus on the problem-solving aspect without being overwhelmed by cluttered visuals or complex mechanics.

One of the strengths of Minimalism lies in its aesthetic. The clean, uncomplicated art style perfectly complements the meditative pace of the gameplay, offering an experience that is both relaxing and intellectually stimulating. The puzzles are well-crafted, with each level presenting a new challenge that gradually increases in complexity. The sense of progression is rewarding, as players learn to think in abstract ways to solve the puzzles. The game’s soundtrack, which is soft and ambient, further enhances the calming atmosphere, creating a truly immersive environment for puzzle lovers.

However, the game’s simplicity can also be a double-edged sword. While the minimalist approach is refreshing, it may feel repetitive for some players as the puzzles become predictable and lack variety. The game’s pacing can sometimes be slow, and the absence of a clear narrative or additional gameplay features may leave some players craving more depth or a sense of purpose beyond the puzzles themselves.

Despite these shortcomings, Minimalism offers an enjoyable and serene experience for those who appreciate understated design and thoughtful challenges. Its simplicity and elegance make it a pleasant choice for players seeking a calm, no-frills puzzle game.

Score: 75/100

[b]Briefly: [i]Minimalism[/i] is a semi-hardcore platformer with abstract visuals and clumsy controls.[/b]

This is a hard one to review. While I think [i]Minimalism[/i] was altogether a good game, it does have its quirks and qualms.

[h1]Square McSquareface[/h1]

In visuals, [i]Minimalism[/i] goes all the way to abstract: even the main character is just a big square. The rest of the cast is rather typical: avoid spikes, sawblades and bullets (i.e. arrows).

Gameplay is also usual: grab everything that's not locked in place and escape to the next level. You have to grab at least the keys, but all levels host a whole bunch of Japanese and Roman letters to find, each of which doubles as an achievement.

Controls, on the other hand, range from unconfortable to unique.

[h1]Full controller support: yes but...[/h1]

Initially, I played [i]Minimalism[/i] with an Xbox controller. You jump with 'A' but as for other movement controls, the game recognizes only the stick: D-pad doesn't work.

This would be fine, but McSquareface has only one mode of movement: full speed.

Precision platformers commonly are played with gamepads because one can use the stick to control their speed precisely to time their jumps and avoid traps gracefully. You lose all that control if you can't control the movement speed. Early platformers did this with a specific run- (or more rarely walk-) button but that's non-existent here.

Combined with some really tight corridors filled with spikes and pixel-wide platforms, frustration is guaranteed.

Consequently, as you could only move if you pushed the stick all the way, playing with keyboard was actually easier and more natural. You can't change the keys though, so you are stuck with Space for jump.

[h1]Unique wall-jumps[/h1]

[i]Minimalism[/i] handles its wall-jumps in a quirky fashion. If you touch a wall, you'll slide down slowly, even if not moving towards the wall.

Pressing jump button and keeping it down will jump you full speed towards the opposite direction like a regular jump. Releasing the jump button while in air will then stop the square in place and allow for air control. This works surprisingly well, though sudden slowing at the wall can be startling and mess up your trajectory.

[h1]Strong level design[/h1]

Since death respawns you at the start of the level, it's good that the levels are not that big.

Generally, the levels are well designed, challenging, and fair: it's usually your own fault if you mess up and die.

However, at times the controls make this frustrating and rage-inducing. Also, the game introduces falling spike traps: these totally lack the visual cue that once you step near them, they will fall and kill you. This either stops your fast pace, as you either have to [b]a)[/b] stop to check each spike lest they fall or not, or [b]b)[/b] [i]die[/i] to the falling spike and feel a need to berserk the controller to the wall as you respawn at the start of the level.

Why they had to put such an unfair device into the game?

[h1]Conclusions[/h1]

As for technical side, I experienced screen-tearing and twitching, while retaining 60fps at those times. This graphics bug would haunt most of the levels at seemingly random intervals.

Music is pleasant, soothing the upcoming frustration.

After numerous attempts and annoyance at the controls, I managed to beat the game after 2 hours and 45 minutes. For $1 game (and I bought it with -75% coupon) the length was decent.

The achievements, while nice, are a bit on the spammy side, as there are over 100 characters to collect. I suppose they will at least make nice profile decorations.

I would recommend [i]Minimalism[/i] for gamers who love tough platformers. But only them: the rest of you should beware of the lousy control scheme.

[h2]ENGLISH & SPANISH REVIEW[/h2]

[h2]ENGLISH REVIEW[/h2]

"Minimalism" is a game where you play as a box that has to navigate different kinds of obstacles to reach a magical portal at the end of the game that will return you to the real world, where you'll get all your achievements written in Japanese Hiragana characters to display on your profile.

The game is extremely basic, but don't let its simple design fool you. Many challenges await you in there; one of the first is learning how your character's square body reacts to holding down keys for a certain amount of time, its exquisite hitbox, how it interacts with its environment and traps—which are very diverse, ranging from static spikes, vertically moving spikes, spinning spikes placed on a small platform you have to cross, spikes that drop out of nowhere (FCK!), and arrows too.

If you're doing this for the Hiragana achievements, which is why almost all of us bought this sub-$1 game, I must warn you that this isn't a game where you just click "Next" and they hand them to you. No, here you'll have to earn your Japanese letters with grit and hard work. They will be suspended in the air, eager for you to grab them, protected by a stern triangle-shaped guard. Therefore, it's a difficult game where you'll need to arm yourself with patience and perseverance, but it's totally worth it.

In short, if you want easy achievements, don't play this game. But if you truly have the willpower and determination to get them, give it a try—you won't regret it.

Minimalism by PixelMouse is a platformer that lives up to its name by stripping away any superfluous elements and focusing purely on tight, precise gameplay. From the moment you start, it’s clear that this game is about honing your skills and mastering each level rather than being distracted by flashy graphics or complex storylines. The premise is simple: control a small cube and navigate through a series of increasingly challenging levels by collecting keys and reaching the exit. While this may sound straightforward, the difficulty ramps up steadily, testing your reflexes, timing, and problem-solving skills in ways that feel rewarding rather than frustrating. The game’s design encourages you to think carefully about each move and to learn from your mistakes, making every success feel hard-earned and satisfying.

Visually, Minimalism embraces a stark, geometric aesthetic that perfectly aligns with its gameplay philosophy. The clean, uncluttered visuals mean there’s nothing pulling your attention away from the level design and the challenge ahead. The cube you control and the obstacles you face are all rendered in simple shapes and solid colors, creating a consistent and focused visual experience. While the art style might be too bare-bones for players who enjoy rich, detailed environments, it works incredibly well for what the game sets out to achieve: pure gameplay enjoyment without distractions. The minimal color palette and design also contribute to a smooth, fast-paced experience, as the game runs fluidly even on modest hardware.

The sound design in Minimalism is similarly understated but effective. The soundtrack is subtle, featuring ambient tones that never overpower the action but help build an immersive atmosphere. Sound effects are minimal but precise, giving clear feedback on your movements and interactions within the game world. This restraint in audio design complements the visual minimalism and gameplay focus, ensuring that every element serves to enhance concentration and immersion rather than detract from it.
